title: Fish a stir bar out through a narrow flask neck on a magnetic retriever, then slide its magnet up to drop it in a beaker
instruction: Take the stir bar out of the flask with the magnetic retriever and drop it into the beaker: hold the tube and slide its magnet up by the ring to let the bar go, then lift the retriever out of the beaker. Do not tip, pour or move the flask.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. Flask: DURAN narrow-neck Erlenmeyer flask, 500 mL (DWK 212164404), clear borosilicate glass, 105 mm across the base, 180 mm tall, neck 34 mm outside with a bore of about 29 mm, standing free with its base centred at (30, -8) on a 105 mm taped circle; 300 mL of tap water in it. Stir bar: SP Bel-Art Spinbar F37109-0010, red PTFE-coated Alnico octagon bar with a pivot ring, 25.4 x 8 mm, about 4 g, lying flat on the flask's floor at its centre, along x. Retriever: SP Bel-Art stirring bar positioner/retriever H37780-0000, white polyethylene tube 15.9 mm across and 305 mm long with a magnet rod sliding 30 mm inside it; the rod ends above the tube in a 10 mm stem and a 22 mm ring handle. It lies flat on the table along y, its middle at (16, -5), tip toward -y, the magnet rod pushed fully down. Beaker: PYREX 1000-250, 250 mL low-form borosilicate beaker, 70 mm across, 95 mm tall, empty, centred at (30, +3). For real trials (not simulated): a 40 x 30 x 2 cm polypropylene catch tray under flask and beaker. The arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: Flask upset (latched for the whole trial): if the flask tilts more than 30 degrees from upright at any moment, or its base slides off the taped circle by more than 2 cm, the trial scores 0. Otherwise the best of: 0.25 the retriever's tip went into the flask, below its rim; 0.5 the bar, picked up with the retriever's tip inside the flask, had its lowest point at least 3 cm above the flask's floor; 0.75 the whole bar was at least 1 cm above the rim; 1.0 the bar lies inside the beaker (its middle within 2 cm of the floor, still), let go by sliding the magnet rod up 12 mm or more inside the tube while the bar was over the beaker's opening, no part of the retriever's tube inside the flask or the beaker, the tube at least 1 cm and every fingertip at least 3 cm from the bar's corners, flask and beaker within 10 degrees of upright, held for 1 s. A bar dragged through the glass from outside the flask counts for nothing. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: a phone filming from the side at table height for tilts, the bar's heights against the flask's 180 mm and the rod's slide; a photo of the bar in the beaker; a ruler for the circle and the clearances.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz; convex glass walls; water not simulated (its mass is). The magnet is an approximation, acting only with no glass between tube and bar: within 6 mm, rod down, the bar is placed along the tube on a rigid joint; lost on reaching the neck's glass or if pushed 3 mm off its place, let go when the free-sliding rod rises 12 mm, re-caught once 1 cm from the tube. Estimates: tool masses, ring size, 30 mm rod travel, 4 g bar, 29 mm bore.
context: Most solutions in research labs are made up on a magnetic stirrer, and the PTFE stir bar has to come out before the flask is emptied, made up to volume or autoclaved. It cannot be tipped out without pouring the solution with it, so labs fish it out with a magnetic retriever: a tube with a magnet rod inside that picks the bar up while pushed down and lets it go when slid up inside the tube by its ring. The bar clings along the side of the tube (as in the maker's photo), so tube and bar together barely pass the flask's neck: the tool has to come up straight and centred, or the rim strips the bar off. Over the beaker, the magnet rod is slid up inside the tube by its ring and the bar drops off.
